explanations.answer: Cut themselves or shave their foreheads
explanations.explanation: That's the rule, baker. Moses says Israel must not cut themselves or shave their foreheads on behalf of the dead. It's the very first instruction in the chapter, right after he calls them sons of the LORD their God. Loss is heavy, and I think that's a tender place for a rule to land.

explanations.answer: Tear their clothes and wear sackcloth
explanations.explanation: Torn clothes and sackcloth do sound like mourning, so I see why that one caught your eye. But Moses doesn't mention either one here. What he says is don't cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead. I'd have picked the familiar one too, friend. I once spent a whole afternoon sure I knew the recipe, and the dough had other plans.

explanations.answer: Mourn for more than seven days
explanations.explanation: Seven days is a nice tidy number, but Moses gives no length of mourning in this passage. He gives a rule about what not to do: don't cut yourselves or shave your foreheads on behalf of the dead. No calendar, no countdown timer. Just what to leave alone.

explanations.answer: They are a people holy to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Moses ties it straight to who they are: "…for you are a people holy to the LORD your God." (Deuteronomy 14:2) Back in verse 1 he had just called them sons of the LORD their God. I think that's the heart of it. Whose they are shapes what they do.

explanations.answer: Only the priests may mourn like that
explanations.explanation: Priests don't come up in these two verses at all. Moses gives his reason in plain words: Israel is a people holy to the LORD their God. He's speaking to the whole people, with no special badge for one group. So the answer was sitting right there in verse 2, friend.

explanations.answer: The land they live in isn't theirs yet
explanations.explanation: The land never comes up in this reason. Moses says Israel is a people holy to the LORD their God, and that the LORD has chosen them out of all the peoples on the face of the earth (Deuteronomy 14:2). That's the whole reason on the table, friend. It's about who they belong to, not where they're standing.

It's right there: "The LORD has chosen you to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth." (Deuteronomy 14:2) Prized possession, friend. I know a little about being picked up out of a bin of bargains, so that line gets me right in the apron.

This one is actually true. Moses says the LORD has chosen Israel to be a people for His prized possession out of all the peoples on the face of the earth. That's about as big a circle as you can draw. Read it again and you'll see those words sitting right in verse 2.

explanations.answer: It has a split hoof and chews the cud
explanations.explanation: Two checks, and the animal has to pass both. Moses says, "You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud." (Deuteronomy 14:6) One out of two doesn't get through the door. He's about to show us exactly that.

explanations.answer: It has horns and grazes in herds
explanations.explanation: Horns and herds sound like a good guess, but Moses doesn't use either one. His test is about the hoof and the cud. He says, "You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud." (Deuteronomy 14:6) Nothing about horns, friend.

explanations.answer: It has a thick coat and eats grass
explanations.explanation: Coats and grass don't show up in Moses' test. He looks at the feet and the chewing. He says, "You may eat any animal that has a split hoof divided in two and that chews the cud." (Deuteronomy 14:6) Two checks, both about the hoof and the cud.

Chewing the cud sounds like it should settle it, I know. But that's only half of the test. Moses says the camel, the rabbit and the rock badger chew the cud, yet they don't have a divided hoof, so they are unclean for Israel (Deuteronomy 14:7). An animal has to pass both tests, friend. It's like a two-key lock: one key turns, the door still doesn't open.

Right, and here's why. The camel, the rabbit and the rock badger chew the cud, but they don't have a divided hoof. Moses calls them unclean for Israel (Deuteronomy 14:7). One check passed and one missed means they stay off the list. Picture rolling up to a job interview in a sharp jacket and no pants, because dressed halfway is not dressed.

explanations.answer: It does not chew the cud
explanations.explanation: Right. The pig passes the hoof check, since it has a divided hoof. But Moses says it does not chew the cud, so it is unclean for Israel. That second check is the one it misses.

That's a guess about the pig's habits, and Moses doesn't say it. The reason he gives is simple: the pig has a divided hoof, but it does not chew the cud. That's the whole reason in the text. I try not to add my own reasons to the Word, friend.

explanations.answer: It rolls around in the mud
explanations.explanation: Mud never comes up in this verse. Moses says the pig has a divided hoof, though it does not chew the cud, and that's why it's unclean. The text gives that reason and no other. So I stick to the cud.

Moses gives two separate rules about the pig: "You must not eat its meat or touch its carcass." (Deuteronomy 14:8) One is about eating the meat. The other is about touching the carcass. So the rule reaches past the dinner table.

This one is true, and the rule is bigger than you might think. Moses says of the pig, "You must not eat its meat or touch its carcass." (Deuteronomy 14:8) Eating and touching, both. Read that last bit again and you'll catch it.

Fins and scales, both. Moses says, "Of all the creatures that live in the water, you may eat anything with fins and scales…" (Deuteronomy 14:9) Anything in the water without fins and scales is unclean for them. One test for the whole sea.

Shells are a fair guess for something living in the water, but Moses doesn't use them as the test. He says Israel may eat anything with fins and scales (Deuteronomy 14:9). Without fins and scales, the creature is unclean for them. The word you're after is scales, friend.

Claws don't make it into Moses' water test. He says, "…you may eat anything with fins and scales…" and anything without both is unclean for them (Deuteronomy 14:9, 10). So the missing word is scales. That's the whole test, friend.

Easy to flip that one, but Moses says the opposite. "All flying insects are unclean for you; they may not be eaten." (Deuteronomy 14:19) Not clean, and not on the menu. It's a short verse, and it's very clear.

False, and you nailed it, baker! Moses says, "All flying insects are unclean for you; they may not be eaten." (Deuteronomy 14:19) Not one bug with wings gets a pass. Mosquito, moth, whatever's buzzing around your porch light: all off the menu. Honestly, my ovens stay bug free, so I've never had to worry.

Moses says, "You are not to eat any carcass; you may give it to the foreigner residing within your gates, and he may eat it, or you may sell it to a foreigner." (Deuteronomy 14:21) So it goes either way, given or sold. Nothing in that line says to toss it out.

The Levite does come up in this chapter, but not here. In verse 21 the carcass goes to the foreigner living within their gates. Moses says they may give it to him, or sell it to a foreigner. The Levite's turn comes later in the sermon, friend.

Priests aren't named anywhere in this rule. Moses says Israel may give the carcass to the foreigner residing within their gates, or sell it to a foreigner (Deuteronomy 14:21). So the blank is foreigner. Keep your eyes on that word, friend.

A tenth is what Moses says: "You must be sure to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from your fields." (Deuteronomy 14:22) It's a share of all of it, and it's every year. Ten cookies on the tray, one set aside. That's the picture, friend.

A third is close to a number that does show up later. In verse 28 Moses says every three years Israel brings a tithe and lays it up within their gates (Deuteronomy 14:28). But the amount he names here is a tenth of all the produce from their fields each year (Deuteronomy 14:22). Three and ten can blur together, friend.

Half would be a big pile of produce. But Moses says to set aside a tenth of all the produce brought forth each year from their fields (Deuteronomy 14:22). One tenth, every year. That's the number to hold on to.

Eat it is right. Moses says Israel is to eat that tenth in the LORD's presence, at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name (Deuteronomy 14:23). The grain, the new wine and oil, and the firstborn of the herds and flocks all go on that table. This tithe comes with a seat before the LORD.

Burning isn't what Moses asks for here. Look at the verb: Israel is to eat that tenth, along with the firstborn of the herds and flocks, in the presence of the LORD their God (Deuteronomy 14:23). The place is the one He will choose as a dwelling for His Name. So this one is a meal, friend. Bring an appetite.

No king appears in this instruction. Moses says Israel is to eat the tenth in the presence of the LORD their God, at the place He will choose as a dwelling for His Name (Deuteronomy 14:23). The tithe goes to the table in that place, friend.

explanations.answer: To fear the LORD their God always
explanations.explanation: Moses gives the reason himself: "…so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." (Deuteronomy 14:23) The eating happens in His presence, and the learning comes with it. Always, friend, not just on feast days.

explanations.answer: To remember their years in the desert
explanations.explanation: The desert is a big part of Moses' sermon overall, but this verse names a different lesson. He says they eat the tithe in the LORD's presence "…so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." (Deuteronomy 14:23) That's the lesson the text gives.

explanations.answer: To work their fields a little harder
explanations.explanation: Harder fieldwork would have me worn out just thinking about it, and I'm the one standing on a gold base all day. But Moses doesn't say that. He says the eating is "…so that you may learn to fear the LORD your God always." (Deuteronomy 14:23) The lesson is about the LORD.

That's what Moses says. If the place is too far to carry what the LORD has blessed them with, they can exchange it for money, take the money in hand, and go to the place the LORD will choose (Deuteronomy 14:24, 25). A lighter load for the road, friend.

This one is true. Moses says that if the distance is too great, "…then exchange it for money, take the money in your hand, and go to the place the LORD your God will choose." (Deuteronomy 14:25) So the money goes with them on the trip.

Cattle and sheep are on the list, so I see why it felt true. But the list keeps going. Moses says they may spend the money on "cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish." (Deuteronomy 14:26) That last part opens the whole market up.

Right, it isn't only cattle and sheep. Moses says, "…you may spend the money on anything you desire: cattle, sheep, wine, strong drink, or anything you wish." (Deuteronomy 14:26) Cattle and sheep are just the start of the list. Anything you wish, friend.

Rejoice is the word. Moses says, "You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household." (Deuteronomy 14:26) A feast, a family and gladness, all in one verse. I love a sermon with a party in it.

Fasting is the opposite of what's happening in this verse. Moses says they are to feast in the presence of the LORD and rejoice with their household (Deuteronomy 14:26). A feast and a fast don't go together, friend. The blank is rejoice.

Praying is a good thing, but it isn't the word in this verse. Moses says, "You are to feast there in the presence of the LORD your God and rejoice with your household." (Deuteronomy 14:26) So the word that fits the blank is rejoice.

explanations.answer: He has no portion or inheritance
explanations.explanation: That's the reason Moses gives: "…since he has no portion or inheritance among you." (Deuteronomy 14:27) He tells Israel not to neglect the Levite within their gates, and this is why. As Moses lays out the feast, someone is still on his mind.

explanations.answer: He is too old to farm the land
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything about the Levite's age or his farming. The reason it gives is that he has no portion or inheritance among them (Deuteronomy 14:27). That's the reason on the page, and I won't add one of my own.

explanations.answer: He guards the gates of the city
explanations.explanation: Guarding gates isn't mentioned. Moses says the Levite is within their gates, meaning in their towns, and he gives this reason not to neglect him: he has no portion or inheritance among them (Deuteronomy 14:27). Nothing there about a job at the gate, friend.

Moses says, "…bring a tenth of all your produce for that year and lay it up within your gates." (Deuteronomy 14:28) Within their gates means right at home in their own towns. This time the tithe stays close instead of making the trip.

The fields are where the produce grows, but that isn't where Moses says to lay it up. He says to bring the tenth of that year's produce and lay it up within their gates (Deuteronomy 14:28). Gates mean their towns, friend.

No king or storehouse shows up here. Moses says to bring a tenth of all their produce for that year and lay it up within their gates (Deuteronomy 14:28). That's in their own towns. The king isn't part of this verse at all.

explanations.answer: The foreigner and fatherless and widow
explanations.explanation: Moses says, "…the Levite (because he has no portion or inheritance among you), the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow within your gates may come and eat and be satisfied." (Deuteronomy 14:29) Everybody gets a seat at that table. I always say the best part of a full batch is a full table.

explanations.answer: The priests and elders and judges
explanations.explanation: Priests, elders and judges are not on this guest list. Moses names the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow within their gates (Deuteronomy 14:29). They may come and eat and be satisfied. Look at who's at the table, friend.

explanations.answer: The soldiers and the king's servants
explanations.explanation: Soldiers and the king's servants aren't mentioned in these verses. Moses says the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow within their gates may come and eat and be satisfied (Deuteronomy 14:29). That's the whole guest list.

That's how Moses closes it: "And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands." (Deuteronomy 14:29) It comes right after the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow come to eat and be satisfied. A promise of blessing on all the work of their hands.

This one is true. Moses says, "And the LORD your God will bless you in all the work of your hands." (Deuteronomy 14:29) It's the closing line of the chapter. Check that last verse, friend, and you'll see it.
